props.title: The Music Man

sections.content: The 2003 ABC television adaptation of The Music Man (2003) starring Matthew Broderick follows the beloved 1962 film version with Robert Preston, both based on Meredith Willson's 1957 Broadway hit. This made-for-TV version maintains the core story of con man Harold Hill charming a small Iowa town, but lacks the technicolor splendor and dynamic energy of Morton DaCosta's The Music Man. While Broderick brings his signature theatrical charm, he struggles to match Preston's magnetic swagger and rapid-fire delivery in iconic numbers like "Ya Got Trouble" and "76 Trombones."

sections.content: The 2003 adaptation reflects a broader trend of attempting to recreate classic musicals for television, following in the footsteps of Annie (1999) and South Pacific (2001). While these productions make beloved musicals accessible to new audiences, they often suffer in comparison to their theatrical predecessors. The TV format typically constrains the scope and spectacle that make golden age musicals so magical. This is particularly evident in the 2003 Music Man's more modest production numbers and simplified choreography compared to the 1962 film's elaborate sequences.

The evolution of "The Music Man" across different eras provides fascinating insight into changing performance styles and production values. While Guys and Dolls (1955) and Oklahoma! (1955) successfully translated Broadway's golden age to film with minimal compromise, later TV adaptations like Annie (1999) and Once Upon a Mattress (2005) often feel scaled down. The 2003 Music Man falls into this pattern, though it deserves credit for maintaining most of the original's wit and charm. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Classic Musical Adaptations

sections.content: The 2003 Music Man exists in an interesting middle ground between faithful recreation and contemporary reimagining. Unlike more radical reinterpretations like Chicago (2002) or Moulin Rouge! (2001), it aims to recreate the original's wholesome charm for modern audiences. This connects it to other traditionally-minded adaptations like The Sound of Music Live! (2013) and Peter Pan Live! (2014), which prioritize accessibility and familiarity over innovation. However, this conservative approach often results in productions that feel like well-intentioned but pale imitations of their inspirations.
